knowledgePattern: Expose a squared quadratic and count distinct roots at two levels

hints.title: Look for a square
hints.body: Factor the first three terms as far as possible before attempting to solve the quartic.
hints.recap: A repeated composite expression can be treated as one quantity.
hints.pitfall: Check the sign of the parameter before taking square roots.
hints.pause: Rewrite the equation and separate every real square-root branch.

recall.reminder: A repeated composite expression can be treated as one quantity.

hints.title: Count roots in each branch
hints.body: Apply the quadratic discriminant to the branch equations, then check whether different branches can share a root.
hints.recap: A positive discriminant gives two distinct real roots; equality gives a repeated root.
hints.pitfall: Four roots counted with multiplicity are not necessarily four distinct roots.
hints.pause: Find and combine the strict parameter conditions.

recall.reminder: A positive discriminant gives two distinct real roots; equality gives a repeated root.

solution:
1. The equation is [x(x−2a)]2=a. If a<0, there are no real solutions. If a=0, only x=0 is a solution. Hence four distinct roots require a>0.

2. For positive a, taking both square-root signs gives x2−2ax=a or x2−2ax=−a. The two equations cannot share a root because their right sides differ.

3. The first quadratic has discriminant 4a2+4a>0. The second has two distinct real roots precisely when 4a2−4a>0.

4. Thus a2>a. With a>0, this is equivalent to a4>a, hence a3>1 and a>1. At a=1, a repeated quadratic root gives only three distinct roots, so equality is excluded. Answer A.
